summary: The HOKEY working group aimed to cut the authentication delay when a device moves between points of attachment. This informational RFC describes the architecture covering early authentication and reuse of cryptographic material.

eli5.summary: When you move to a new Wi-Fi spot, logging in again takes time. This describes ways to make the move smooth.

questions: how to reduce authentication delay during handover
subtitle: Architecture for reducing authentication delay when a device moves between network attachment points.

tldr.problem: When a mobile device moves from one network access point to another, re-authentication using full EAP causes noticeable delays and may drop active sessions, especially when moving to visited networks.
tldr.mechanism: The HOKEY architecture defines two complementary strategies: early authentication (pre-placing keying material on candidate attachment points before handover) and re-authentication (using keys derived from an initial authentication to speed up re-authentication). These reduce handover latency by avoiding repeated full EAP exchanges.
tldr.outcome: Devices can maintain service continuity during handover without excessive authentication delays, improving user experience for mobile and wireless scenarios.

facts.label: Authentication protocols supported
facts.value: EAP re-authentication (ER), early authentication (direct/indirect pre-auth), AAK

facts.label: Server components
facts.value: EAP Server, ER Server, ER/AAK Server

today: RFC 6697 is an Informational RFC that defines the HOKEY architecture for fast handover authentication. It has not been obsoleted and remains the reference for understanding how EAP re-authentication and early authentication can be integrated into mobile and wireless networks.

sections.title: The Handover Delay Problem
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) is widely used for authentication in access networks, from Wi-Fi to cellular. However, when a mobile device (the peer) moves from one point of attachment to another, it must be re-authenticated. If a full EAP exchange repeats, multiple round trips between the peer and the EAP server occur, creating noticeable delay. This delay is worse when the new access point is in a visited (foreign) network rather than the peer's home network, because extra procedural steps and longer network distances add latency.

The HOKEY Working Group addresses this by defining an architecture that supports two approaches: (1) EAP re-authentication (ER), which reuses cryptographic material from the initial authentication to enable single-round-trip authentication, and (2) early authentication, which pre-establishes keys at candidate attachment points before the device actually moves. Both approaches avoid repeating expensive full EAP exchanges.
sections.eli5: EAP authentication can take many back-and-forth messages between your device and a home server, causing delay. HOKEY speeds this up by letting you reuse part of your first login or by pre-logging into the next spot before you move there.

sections.title: Core Architecture Components
sections.content:
The HOKEY architecture consists of five main components:

The Peer is the mobile device seeking to authenticate and move between access points.

The Authenticator is part of the access point infrastructure. The Serving Authenticator (SAP) is where the peer is currently attached; the Candidate Authenticator (CAP) is where the peer will attach next.

The EAP Server terminates the full EAP exchange and creates authentication keys (the Master Session Key, or MSK).

The ER (Re-Authentication) Server uses keys derived from the initial authentication to perform faster re-authentication, eliminating the need to contact the home EAP server on every handover.

The ER/AAK Server combines ER functionality with Authenticated Anticipatory Keying (AAK), allowing it to derive and push pre-established session keys to candidate attachment points for immediate use on handover.

These components are organized to minimize communication with distant home servers and reduce round-trip latency by placing re-authentication capacity close to the peer.
sections.eli5: The peer (your device) talks to authenticators at its current and next spots. The EAP Server at home does full authentication once. An ER Server nearby does fast re-authentication. An ER/AAK Server can pre-place keys at the next spot before you move there.

sections.title: Two Functional Approaches: ER and Early Authentication
sections.content:
EAP Re-authentication (ER) operates after initial authentication is complete. The EAP server derives a re-authentication root key (rRK) from the initial EAP Master Session Key and distributes it to local ER servers via AAA protocols. When the peer hands over to a new access point, it performs a single-round-trip ERP exchange with the local ER server, using the rRK to derive new session keys in a fraction of the time needed for full EAP. The peer only contacts a home server if the local ER server is unavailable.

Early Authentication pre-establishes keys on candidate attachment points before the peer moves. Three variants exist: (1) Direct pre-authentication, where the peer discovers and directly initiates EAP authentication with candidate access points (using IP transport); (2) Indirect pre-authentication, where the serving authenticator brokers the exchange; and (3) Authenticated Anticipatory Keying (AAK), where an ER/AAK server derives pre-established Master Session Keys (pMSKs) and pushes them to candidate attachment points. AAK is the most efficient because it reuses derived keys rather than repeating full EAP exchanges.

Both approaches can be combined: ER for immediate local re-authentication and early authentication (especially AAK) to make the next handover even faster.
sections.eli5: ER lets you reuse part of your first login to authenticate in one quick exchange with a nearby server instead of contacting home. Early auth pre-places a login ticket at your next spot so you can use it immediately when you arrive.

sections.title: Design Objectives
sections.content:
The HOKEY architecture aims to achieve four key design goals:

Minimized communications with home servers: By placing ER and AAK servers in local domains, peers should only need to communicate with local servers, not distant home servers, during handover. Home contact is needed only during initial authentication.

Minimized user interaction: After initial authentication (which may require the user to enter credentials), subsequent re-authentication and handovers should happen transparently without user prompts or dialogs.

Efficient local domain name discovery: Peers need to discover the domain name of local ER servers to derive re-authentication keys. The architecture integrates this discovery with ERP implicit bootstrapping to avoid extra handover delays.

Improved deployment scalability: ER servers and AAK servers should not need to be co-located with AAA servers or proxies, giving administrators flexibility in network design and reducing scalability bottlenecks.
sections.eli5: The goals are: keep login servers close, never ask the user again, discover nearby servers quickly, and let operators place these servers anywhere without tying them to other servers.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The HOKEY architecture supports several deployment scenarios, each with different characteristics:

Simple re-authentication: The peer remains at the same access point but re-authenticates (e.g., after a timeout). The access point acts as both serving and candidate authenticator, and ER can be used locally.

Intra-domain handover: The peer moves between two authenticators in the same domain. The peer communicates with the ER server within the same local network, avoiding any home server contact.

Inter-domain handover: The peer moves between different administrative domains. It may communicate with ER servers in the current domain, the previous domain, and the home domain to manage credentials across domain boundaries.

Inter-technology handover: The peer moves between heterogeneous networks (e.g., from Wi-Fi to cellular). If the networks are administratively in the same or overlapping domains, intra-domain ER handover is sufficient. Otherwise, full EAP authentication may be required.

The architecture supports all four scenarios using the same core components, with only the network topology and ER server placement varying between scenarios.
sections.eli5: The same architecture handles staying at one spot and logging in again, moving within your company's network, moving to a partner network, or switching from Wi-Fi to phone data.
